en: The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of King Mūrdhaja Spoken by the Buddha,

Scroll One. Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīladharma, Dharma Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, Imperially Appointed Grand Officer of the Court of Ceremonial and Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
Monk of Purple Robes, Subject Shi Hu, and others, in accordance with the Imperial Decree.

At one time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time, King Prasenajit, the Great Sovereign of the Kingdom of Kośala, came to where the Buddha was. Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“World-Honored One, when you were formerly seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, how did you practice giving and perform various meritorious deeds?
The Buddha said,
“Great King!”

Let us set aside the events of the distant past eons. I shall now relate for you the causes and conditions of how I practiced the perfection of giving while seeking *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* within this present Bhadrakalpa; listen attentively and apply your minds with great care as I speak to you.
"Great King!

At the beginning of this kalpa, when the human lifespan was immeasurable years, there was a king named Puṣpottara. Suddenly, a fleshy growth like a tumor appeared upon the crown of that king's head; it was as soft as tūla-cotton and like fine cotton cloth, and it caused him no pain or distress."

Once it had matured, it spontaneously split open, and a boy was born, possessing the most excellent physical marks, upright and beautiful to behold; his body was like the color of gold, his head bore whorls of hair like a wondrous parasol, his two arms were rounded and long, his forehead was broad and even, his eyebrows extended far, his nose was high and straight, and all parts of his body, from top to bottom, were perfectly complete, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man.

Once the boy was born, he entered the palace; there were sixty thousand palace women and attendants among the king’s retinue, and upon seeing the boy, their breasts spontaneously overflowed with milk, and each said:
"I shall nourish the crown prince."
Because of this, he was given a name and called "My Nourisher" (Māndhātṛ). Others said,
"Since this prince was born from the crown of [his father's] head, he should be named 'Crown-Born' (Mūrdhaja)."
From this, he was called Mūrdhaja (Born from the Crown) or sometimes Māndhātṛ (Nourished by Me).
While Prince Mūrdhaja was still in the stage of a youth, six Śakras passed away during his time in play and amusement;
while he was in the stage of a crown prince, another six Śakras passed away.
On one occasion, the Prince departed from the royal palace and traveled through the streets and marketplaces of the people, observing them in succession.

Later, King Puṣyada suddenly fell ill; his attendants served him with flowers, fruits, roots, sprouts, and medicinal decoctions to treat him, yet despite their diligent efforts, his illness showed no improvement.
The king immediately issued an edict to his ministers and officials, saying:
"You must quickly perform the royal consecration for the crown prince.
Having received these orders, the ministers and officials dispatched messengers to the prince's location, who addressed the prince as follows:
"The Father King lies bedridden with illness; despite efforts to treat him, there has been no improvement. He summoned the Crown Prince, commanding: 'Come now at once to receive the consecration.
When the messenger reached the midpoint of his journey, the King had already passed away."
At that time, the ministers and officials again dispatched messengers who followed one after another to the Prince, saying to him:
"The Father King has passed away; Prince, come quickly to receive the royal consecration."
At that time, Prince Mūrdhaja reflected to himself:
"The Father King has already passed away; what use is it for me to rush there?
Then, after the various ministers and assistants had deliberated, one high-ranking attendant approached the prince and said:
"O Crown Prince!
We pray that you will come here quickly to receive the royal consecration.
The Crown Prince replied:
"If I am destined to preside over the throne of the True Dharma King, he shall come here and perform my consecration.
A close minister spoke again:
"Crown Prince!"

Regarding the conferral of empowerment, there are many ritual procedures; namely, one ought to provide a precious lion throne, silk canopies, and jeweled crowns. As for these necessary requirements, how could such a person possibly prepare them according to the ritual laws?
"Furthermore, it is customary to perform the rite of consecration within the royal city; therefore, the Crown Prince should proceed to the palace so that the King may be granted the consecration.
The Crown Prince replied, "If I am destined to preside over the throne of a righteous Dharma-king, everything required shall arrive of its own accord."

At that time, Prince Mūrdhaja had a yakṣa guide named Nīvara who, by means of his supernatural power, pursued the lion throne, the silk canopy, the jeweled crown, and all other necessities, even including cities and villages, placing them all before the prince;
all who beheld this marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.

"Then his ministers, subjects, and the powerful military forces, holding exquisite silk scarves and according to the rite of consecration, desired to bestow the empowerment upon the crown prince, and spoke these words:
'Crown Prince!'"
"You should bestow the consecration.
Then the Prince said:
"Why should I now use human silks for the rite of consecration to bind upon my head?"

"If I am destined to preside over the throne of a righteous Dharma King, there shall surely be a celestial, exquisite silk cloth to bind upon my head. Subsequently, a particularly wonderful celestial silk cloth spontaneously descended from the heavens for the purpose of his consecration, whereby he presided over the rank of a Wheel-Turning King.

Immediately, the seven treasures appeared according to the occasion—namely, the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the mani-jewel treasure, the woman-treasure, the treasurer-treasure, and the military commander-treasure—and these seven treasures were all fully present;
furthermore, there were a thousand sons of supreme physical appearance, courageous and fearless, capable of subduing enemy armies.
"At that time there was a city also named Vaiśālī, surrounded on all sides by dense groves of trees beloved by people.
Within those forests, five hundred rishis resided, practicing the meditative concentrations of the five supernatural powers."
At that time, there were many birds, such as cranes and herons, in the forest whose noisy clamor disturbed the meditative concentration he was practicing.
A certain seer named Virūpa (Ugly Face) became enraged and, using incantations, paralyzed the flock of cranes and herons so that all their feathers fell off.
At that time, a flock of herons with broken wings moved slowly along the ground and all approached the gate of King Māndhātṛ.
Just as the king was about to go out and happened to observe the left side of the gate, he asked his attendants:
"For what reason has this flock of herons gathered all together by the side of the gate?"
The attendants replied: "Your Majesty!

Flocks of birds nested in the forest and disturbed his meditative concentration with their clamor; the seer, filled with wrath, cast a spell that caused their wings to fall off, and they have now come crawling along the ground and gathered at the king’s gate."
The king said:
"Why do these rishis have no compassion in their hearts for sentient beings? You should now issue an order that this assembly of rishis be quickly expelled from my realm."
The ministers, having received the command, proclaimed the King’s decree in full before the sages.
At that time, the assembly of sages immediately had this thought:
"Now this Great King rules over the four great continents with supreme sovereignty; we should obey his command and go to the side of Mount Sumeru to dwell among the forest groves."

"At that time, King Mūrdhaja gradually reflected upon, examined, and weighed the various activities appropriate for human beings; having thus reflected upon, examined, and weighed them, he initiated each and every kind of human activity."
When the king went out on an excursion, he first saw people among the common folk plowing and planting in the fields;
having seen this, he asked his attendants, "What is the name of this activity performed by these people?"
The minister addressed the king, saying:
"O Son of Heaven!
This man plows his fields and sows various seeds; he sustains his life according to their growth."
The king said, "As a noble cakravartin king, why should I depend on human cultivation for sustenance? I have seeds produced spontaneously from the heavens.
As soon as King Mūrdhaja thought this, twenty-seven kinds of seeds descended from the sky.
The king then asked the multitude of people,
"By whose power of merit has this been brought about?
The multitude replied:
"This is due to the power of the Devaputra’s merit, which extends to us as well.
Furthermore, as the king proceeded further, he saw farmers sowing seeds for cotton cloth;
having seen this, he asked his ministers, "What is the name of this work being performed by these people?"
The minister addressed the king, saying:
"O Son of Heaven!
This man has planted the seeds of a cotton-tree; once it bears fruit, one may take the cotton and produce cotton cloth."
The King said, "As a noble king, why should I rely on planting cotton seeds in the human world? I have the wondrous seeds of heavenly cotton myself.
As soon as he spoke this thought, the seeds of the wondrous cotton garments descended from heaven.
The king then asked the assembly of people,
"By whose power of merit has this been brought about?
The assembly replied:
"This is due to the power of the Devaputra's merit, which extends to us as well.
Furthermore, as the king proceeded gradually, he saw farmers spinning cotton threads for garments;
having seen this, he asked his ministers, "What is the work being done by these people called?"
The minister addressed the king, saying:
"O Son of Heaven!
This man has taken cotton, spun it into thread, and is about to weave it into a piece of cloth."
The King said, "As a holy king, why should I rely on such human craftsmanship? I have exquisite celestial cotton (*karpāsa*) for my own use.
As soon as he spoke these words, garments of exquisite cotton descended spontaneously from the heavens.
The king then asked the multitude of people,
"By whose power of merit has this been brought about?
The multitude of people replied:
"This is due to the power of the Devaputra’s merit, which extends to us as well.
Furthermore, as the king proceeded gradually, he saw farmers weaving pieces of cotton cloth one after another. Having seen this, he asked his ministers:
"What is the name of this work performed by these men?"
The minister said to the king:
"O Son of Heaven!
This man has set up a loom and is weaving a piece of cotton cloth."
The King said, "As a noble king, why should I rely on human cotton cloth to cover my body? I possess the exquisite celestial cotton garments that adorn me.
As soon as these words were spoken, exquisite celestial cotton garments descended from the heavens of their own accord.
The king then asked the multitude of people,
"By whose power of merit has this been brought about?
The multitude of people replied:
"This is due to the power of the Devaputra's merit, as well as our own.
At that time, King Mūrdhaja, having witnessed this event, gave rise to this thought:
"The power of my own merit has not yet been manifested here."

I have already ruled over this Jambudvīpa within the great outer ocean to the south of Mount Sumeru; it is vast within and shaped like a chariot without, its population is flourishing and secure in peace and prosperity;
furthermore, the lands and cities are magnificent and beautiful, and the people dwelling therein possess wondrous and admirable forms.
I possess seven treasures:

namely, the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the mani-jewel treasure, the woman-treasure, the steward-treasure, and the military-commander treasure; these seven treasures I have all fully attained.
Furthermore, may I have a thousand sons of supreme beauty, courageous and fearless, capable of subduing enemy armies; how wonderful it would be if I possessed such superior power!
Now, I pray that within my palace a rain of gold coins shall fall for seven days, such that not even a single coin falls outside the palace grounds."
As soon as the king thought this, it rained gold coins from the sky within the palace for seven full days, with not a single coin falling outside the palace;
according to the power of the roots of merit and the force of his blessings, he personally experienced the fruit of his fortune through supernatural majesty and virtue.
The king then asked the multitude of people,
"By whose power of merit has this been brought about?
The multitude of people replied:
"The power of the Son of Heaven’s merit.
The King said:

"If it were as you have just described, combined with your own strength, why is it that at this time the heavens do not rain down gold to fill Jambudvīpa, so that all the people might take whatever they desire? Therefore, we know that your past causes are meager and slight."
The Buddha said: "Great King!
While that King Māndhātṛ governed the world according to the True Dharma, six Śakras passed away."
Furthermore, King Mūrdhagata said to the yakṣa general Nīvaraṇaviṣkambhin,
"Where else is there another great continent for me to govern?"
Nīvikā replied, "O Devaputra!

To the east of Mount Sumeru, within the great outer ocean, there is a great continent named Videha; it is broad within and shaped like a half-moon without, with a flourishing population living in peace, security, and abundance."

"Furthermore, the kingdoms and cities are magnificent and beautiful, and the people who dwell there possess exquisite forms worthy of being beheld; Your Majesty should go there and guide them according to what is appropriate.
Then King Mūrdhaja thought to himself:
"I have already ruled over this Jambudvīpa, and I am surrounded by the seven treasures and a thousand sons within my palace; moreover, it has rained gold coins for seven days."
"I have further heard that on the eastern side of Mount Sumeru, within the great outer ocean, there is the continent of Pūrvavideha; I shall now go there to guide and transform its inhabitants.

As soon as the King thought this, his entire body rose into the air, surrounded by eighteen koṭis of troops of superior strength and a thousand sons, with the seven treasures leading the way, and in a single kṣaṇa, he arrived at the eastern continent of Pūrvavideha.
"Great King!

That King Māndhātṛ ruled and transformed the people within that continent for many hundreds of thousands of years. According to the power of the meritorious deeds and wholesome roots performed by each of those sentient beings, he personally experienced the fruits of his own merit through supernatural powers and majestic virtue; in this manner, six Śakras passed away."
"Furthermore, King Māndhātṛ said to the yakṣa general Nīvara:
'Where else is there another great continent for me to rule over?'"
Nemika replied: "O Devaputra!

To the west of Mount Sumeru, within the great outer ocean, there is a great continent named Go-dānīya; it is perfectly circular in shape both inside and out, and its inhabitants are numerous, living in peace, security, and abundance."

"Furthermore, the lands and cities there are magnificent and beautiful, and the people who dwell therein possess wondrous forms worthy of being beheld; Your Majesty should go there to transform and guide them as appropriate.
At that time, King Mūrdhaja reflected to himself:
"I have already ruled over Jambudvīpa, possessing the seven treasures and a thousand sons, and the rain of gold coins has fallen."
I have further arrived here on the continent of Pūrvavideha, where I have governed and transformed the people for many hundreds of thousands of years.
Now I have again heard that there is the continent of Aparagoyānī within the great outer ocean to the west of Mount Sumeru; I shall now go there to provide guidance and transformation.

As soon as the king thought this, he rose into the air with his eighteen koṭis of powerful troops and was surrounded by his thousand sons; escorted by the seven treasures, he arrived in the western continent of Aparagoyānī in a single kṣaṇa.
"Great King!

That King Māndhātṛ governed and transformed the people within that continent for many hundreds of thousands of years. In accordance with the power of the meritorious deeds and wholesome actions performed by each of those sentient beings, he personally experienced the fruits of his merit through his supernatural powers and majestic virtue; in this manner, six Indras passed away."
Furthermore, King Mūrdhagata addressed the yakṣa general Nīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, saying:
"Is there another great continent apart from this one that I may rule?"
Nemika replied: "O Devaputra!

To the north of Mount Sumeru, within the great outer ocean, there is a great continent named Kuru. It is surrounded on all sides and is square in shape; its inhabitants are numerous, peaceful, secure, and enjoy abundant prosperity."
Furthermore, the lands and cities are magnificent and beautiful, and the people dwelling there possess exquisite forms worthy of being beheld;

moreover, the inhabitants of that continent are free from attachment to a self and have no sense of belonging or ownership. Your Majesty should go there and guide them according to what is appropriate.
Then King Mūrdhaja reflected to himself:
"I have already ruled over that Jambudvīpa; I possess the seven treasures and a thousand sons, and there has been a rain of gold coins.
Furthermore, I have gone to Pūrvavideha."
Furthermore, I have come to this continent of Aparagoyānī in the west and have governed and transformed its people for many hundreds of thousands of years.
Now I have heard again that there is the continent of Uttarakuru within the great outer ocean to the north of Mount Sumeru; I shall now go there to provide guidance and transformation.

As soon as the king had this thought, he rose into the air with his eighteen koṭis of troops of superior strength, surrounded by his thousand sons and escorted by the seven treasures, and proceeded toward Uttarakuru, arriving at the side of Mount Sumeru in a single kṣaṇa.
The king saw from afar that the ground in that place was white; having seen it, he immediately asked the yakṣa deity Nīvara:
"For what reason is the ground in this location white?"
Nemika replied: "O Son of Heaven! This is the fragrant rice consumed by the people of Uttarakuru.

It is white in appearance and perfect in both fragrance and flavor; it grows spontaneously without the need for plowing or sowing. The stalks of the rice are four finger-widths long, free of awns or chaff, pure and bright, and ripens according to the seasons."
"The people of that continent do not exert their own labor to obtain food, but simply take it to eat; now when you go there, you too shall take the fragrant rice as your food.
When the king had heard this, he said to his ministers and officials:
"Do you see this white ground?"
The minister replied to the king, saying,
"Indeed, I have seen it.
The king said:

"This is the fragrant rice consumed by the people of Uttarakuru; it is white in appearance and perfect in both fragrance and flavor. It grows spontaneously without the need for plowing or sowing; the stalks are four finger-widths long, without awns or chaff, pure and bright, ripening in due season. The inhabitants of that continent take it for food without expending any effort. You too should go there, take this fragrant rice, and make it your food."
Then King Mūrdhaja, while on the northern side of Mount Sumeru, saw from afar a grove of variously adorned trees, perfectly complete and wondrous to behold. He immediately asked Nairañjanā:
"What kind of grove of variously adorned trees is this?"
Nemika replied: "O Devaputra!

These are the four kinds of *kalpavṛkṣa* (wish-fulfilling trees) belonging to the people of Uttarakuru, namely blue, yellow, red, and white. From these trees emerge exquisite garments of four colors; whenever the men or women of that continent desire such clothing, as soon as the thought arises, the branches of those trees naturally bend downward, allowing them to take as much as they wish."
"Your Majesty shall now go there and likewise wear that robe.
When the king had heard this, he said to his ministers and attendants:
"Do you see these trees of manifold adornments, perfect and without deficiency?"
The minister replied to the king, saying,
"Indeed, I have seen it.
The king said:

"These are the four kinds of *kalpavṛkṣa* (wish-fulfilling trees) belonging to the people of Uttarakuru, namely blue, yellow, red, and white. From these trees emerge exquisite garments of four colors; whenever the men or women of that continent think of such clothing, as soon as the thought arises, the branches of those trees naturally bend downward, allowing them to take as much as they desire."
“You all should go there and wear those robes as well.

“Great King! That King Māndhātṛ ruled and transformed the people of Uttarakuru for many hundreds of thousands of years. According to the power of the meritorious deeds and wholesome roots performed by each of those sentient beings, he personally experienced the fruits of his merit through his supernormal powers and majestic virtue; in this manner, six more Śakras passed away.
Furthermore, King Māndhātṛ said to the yakṣa general Nīvara:
"Is there any other region for me to rule? Nīvara replied:
“O Son of Heaven!
There is no other place ruled by a king.
There are the Thirty-three Heavens, where the inhabitants enjoy long life, beautiful forms, and manifold pleasures, dwelling securely for a long time in lofty and vast palatial towers.”
"How wonderful, O Son of Heaven!
You should go and behold it.
Then King Mūrdhaja thought to himself:
"I have already ruled over that Jambudvīpa, possessing the seven treasures and a thousand sons, and having rained down gold coins;
I have also gone to Pūrvavideha and Aparagoyānī;
and now I have arrived here in Uttarakuru."

Furthermore, I have heard that there are those Trāyastriṃśa gods, who possess long life, beautiful forms, and manifold pleasures; their lofty and vast palaces are secure and stable for dwelling. It would be fitting for me now to go there to behold them.

As soon as the king thought this, he rose into the air with his eighteen koṭis of troops of superior strength, surrounded by his thousand sons and escorted by the seven treasures, and proceeded to the sevenfold golden mountains outside Mount Sumeru.
When that king first arrived at Mount Nimindhara, he found the mountain to be magnificent, exquisite, and beautiful to behold, composed entirely of pure gold.
Therein dwell the gods of the Caturmahārājakāyika heaven, with hosts of devaputras coming and going among them.
The King, with his victorious forces, converted and guided those beings there, and another six Śakras passed away during that time.

Next he arrived at Mount Vinataka; that mountain was magnificent, exquisite, and beautiful to behold, composed entirely of pure gold. Therein lay the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, where hosts of devaputras came and went.
The King, with his victorious forces and troops, converted and guided those beings there, and further six Śakras passed away.

Next he arrived at Horse-Ear Mountain; that mountain was magnificent, exquisite, and beautiful to behold, composed entirely of pure gold, where the Four Great Kings and hosts of devaputras came and went among its peaks.
The King, with his superior power and military forces, converted and guided those beings there, and six more Indras passed away during that time.

Next he arrived at Mount Sudarśana; that mountain was magnificent, exquisite, and beautiful to behold, composed entirely of pure gold. Therein dwelt the gods of the Cāturmahārājika Heaven, with hosts of devaputras coming and going among them.
The King, with his superior power and military forces, converted and guided those beings there, and another six Śakras passed away during this time.

Next, he arrived at Mount Khadiraka; that mountain was magnificent, exquisite, and beautiful to behold, composed entirely of pure gold, and there the gods of the Cāturmahārājika Heaven came and went among its peaks.
The King, with his victorious forces, converted those beings, and another six Śakras passed away during that time.

Next he arrived at Mount Yugaṃdhara; that mountain was magnificent, exquisite, and beautiful to behold, composed entirely of pure gold, where the gods of the Cāturmahārājika Heaven and their hosts of sons moved back and forth.
The King, with his superior power and military forces, converted and guided those beings, and another six Śakras passed away during this time.
*The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of King Mūrdhaja*, Scroll One.
*The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of King Mūrdhaja*, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīladharma, Dharma-transmitting Master and Imperially Conferred Purple Robe, Subject Shi Hu, and others, by imperial decree:
"Furthermore, beyond Mount Yugaṃdhara is Mount Yugandhara; that mountain is majestic, exquisite, and wonderful to behold, being composed entirely of pure gold."
Therein lies the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, where hosts of devaputras come and go.

Mount Sumeru, the King of Mountains, rises loftily above all other peaks; to the east of this king of mountains dwells a Great Heavenly King named Dhṛtarāṣṭra (Holder of the Nation), whose palace city is likewise named Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
That city is exactly two hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth, with a circumference of one thousand yojanas; it is adorned both inside and out, exquisitely beautiful and a sight to behold.
The city has golden walls, half a yojana in height;
atop these golden walls are four battlements made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal;
furthermore, there are double walls leading to the thoroughfares, likewise made of the four precious substances.

The ground within that city was furthermore exceptionally beautiful, wondrous, and magnificently adorned with one hundred and one kinds of painted designs. It was as soft as *tūla* cotton and like exquisite fine cloth; when one set foot upon it, it sank, and when the foot was lifted, it rose again.
Divine *mandārava* flowers were strewn across the ground to a depth of a knee’s length; from time to time, a fragrant breeze blew away the withered blossoms and rained down fresh ones.

The streets within the city were two hundred and fifty yojanas long and twenty-five yojanas wide. The ground was strewn with golden sand, and everywhere it was sprinkled with sandalwood-scented water. Golden cords crisscrossed above, from which hung golden bells and chimes to mark the boundaries of the roadsides.
"On both sides of the streets, there are furthermore various pure ponds and pools, their bottoms spread with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
On the four sides of each pond are four stairways made of the four precious substances; the floors and the steps are likewise fashioned from the four precious substances.

Furthermore, within these ponds and pools, there are pavilions made of the four precious substances interspersed as adornments: if the pavilion is of gold, its pillars and beams are of silver; if the pavilion is of silver, its pillars and beams are of gold; if the pavilion is of lapis lazuli, its pillars and beams are of crystal; and if the pavilion is of crystal, its pillars and beams are of lapis lazuli."
The pool is filled with clear, cool, sweet water;
it is completely covered within by *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers.
Furthermore, various water-birds sport within the pond, emitting wondrous sounds—namely, lofty and distant sounds, pleasing sounds, and exquisite sounds.

Surrounding that pond are various flowering trees and fruit-bearing trees, growing straight, standing upright, and perfectly circular without defect; they are just like a master garland-maker who takes fine thread and, with exquisite skill, arranges and knots it to form a garland—the groves of flowering and fruit-bearing trees are exactly like this.
Furthermore, various kinds of flying birds dwell upon that tree, emitting wondrous sounds—namely, lofty and distant sounds, pleasing sounds, and beautiful, exquisite sounds.

Furthermore, within that palace there are four kinds of *kalpavṛkṣa* trees—blue, yellow, red, and white—from which emerge exquisite garments of those four colors. If any of those celestial males or females should think of such a garment, it arrives in their hands the very moment the thought arises.

Furthermore, within that palace there are various trees of exquisite musical instruments, namely flutes, pipes, lutes, harps, and so forth; whenever those deva males and females desire music, as soon as the thought arises, the instruments sound of their own accord.

Furthermore, within that palace there are various trees of exquisite adornment; from those trees emerge bracelets, anklets, and all manner of fine ornaments for the body. Whenever those devas, whether male or female, think of such ornaments, they arrive in their hands the very moment the thought arises.

Furthermore, within that palace there are four kinds of *suda* food of exquisite flavor—namely, blue, yellow, red, and white—which, when those deva males and females think of such food, arrive in their hands the very moment they give rise to the thought.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of beverages to be drunk, namely: *madhūka* juice, *mṛdvīkā* juice, *kharjūra* juice, and *pānaka* juice, and so forth.

Within that palace were magnificent halls, pavilions, and towers, where hosts of celestial maidens either sat in peaceful repose or moved about in observation. All were provided with various kinds of carriages, garments, and ornaments; the celestial maidens crowded together, beating drums and singing songs, burning various famous incenses, and providing an abundance of food and drink. There, the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, together with his retinue, enjoyed playful delights and happiness, receiving these superior fruits according to the power of their own merit.

"Furthermore, to the south of Mount Sumeru is a Great Heavenly King named Virūḍhaka; his palace city is also named Virūḍhaka. That city is exactly two hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth, with a circumference of one thousand yojanas; it is adorned both inside and out, exquisite and wonderful to behold.
The city has golden walls, half a yojana in height."
Upon the golden walls there are four battlements made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal;
furthermore, there are double walls leading to the pathways, likewise made of the four precious substances.

The ground within that city was exquisitely adorned with one hundred and one kinds of colorful paintings; it was moreover as soft as tūla-cotton and like fine karpāsa cloth, sinking when the foot was set down and rising when the foot was lifted.
Celestial *mandārava* flowers were strewn upon the ground to a depth of one’s knees; from time to time, a fragrant breeze blew away the withered blossoms and rained down new ones.

The city streets were two hundred and fifty *yojanas* long and twenty-five *yojanas* wide; the ground was paved with golden sand, everywhere sprinkled with sandalwood-scented perfumed water, and bordered on both sides by golden cords interlaced with hanging golden bells.
"On both sides of the streets, there are furthermore various pure ponds and pools, their bottoms strewn with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal."
On the four sides of the pond are four stairways made of the four precious substances; its floor and the tiers of steps are likewise fashioned from the four precious substances.

In this manner, six more Śakras passed away.
Furthermore, five hundred sages dwelling on the side of Yugandhara Mountain saw King Mūrdhaja approaching from afar.
Then the Rishi Virūpākṣa, speaking with indignation, said:
"That King of Strife has come here again!
He immediately raised both hands, scooped up water, and sprinkled it upon the vanguard and winged troops, halting their advance.
Then the Lord of the Military Spirits said to the assembly of seers:
"If a practitioner of pure conduct gives rise to anger, his undertakings will not succeed in any place;
this King Mūrdhaja is a great and benevolent king, and you cannot exert your spell-power against him as you did before."
Then King Mūrdhaja gradually approached that place and asked,
"Who is it that is obstructing my army and preventing them from advancing?
The Commander of the Gods replied:
"The assembly of seers has forbidden it.
The king said,
"Among all objects of affection, what is the most supreme?"
The Commander of the Army replied,
"O Venerable Sage, that which you hold dear is having your hair braided.
The King said:
"Now, let their hair be cut off and all of them driven away to serve as my vanguard and escort.
As soon as the king had finished speaking, the hair of that assembly of sages fell away of its own accord, and each naturally came to hold a bow and arrow, leading the way as an advance guard.
Then the Jewel-Woman, the King’s consort, addressed the King, saying:
"O Son of Heaven!
These hosts of sages are practitioners; I pray that Your Majesty will release them."
The king said,
"As you wish. Then,
by the power of their diligence, the assembly of seers realized the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).
King Mūrdhagata, together with his own superior forces and retinue, rose into the air and proceeded further.

That Mount Sumeru rises eighty thousand yojanas from the water and extends eighty thousand yojanas into the water; it is eighty thousand yojanas wide on each of its four sides, with a circumference of three hundred and twenty thousand yojanas. Its base rests upon a ground composed of gold, adorned with various splendors and made of the four precious substances.
That Mount Sumeru has four sides: the eastern side is composed of crystal (sphatika), the western side of white silver, the southern side of lapis lazuli (vaidūrya), and the northern side of gold.

Furthermore, at the four corners of the mountain there are four peaks. Of these, the southeastern peak is exactly one hundred and twenty-five yojanas in length and breadth, five hundred yojanas in circumference, and four and a half yojanas in height;
it is composed of lapis lazuli, and the yakṣa deity Vajrapāṇi dwells therein.
The southwestern peak is exactly one hundred and twenty-five yojanas in length and breadth, five hundred yojanas in circumference, and four and a half yojanas in height;
it is composed of crystal, and the yakṣa deity Vajrapāṇi dwells within it.
The northwest peak is exactly one hundred and twenty-five yojanas in length and breadth, five hundred yojanas in circumference, and four and a half yojanas in height;
it is composed of gold, and the yakṣa deity Vajrapāṇi dwells therein.
The northeastern peak is exactly one hundred and twenty-five yojanas in length and breadth, five hundred yojanas in circumference, and four and a half yojanas in height;
the yakṣa deity Vajrapāṇi dwells therein.
Furthermore, Mount Sumeru has four terraces:
its first terrace extends sixteen thousand yojanas outward and is composed of the four precious substances;
there dwell the gods known as the Dṛḍhaśiras within it.
The second tier is ten thousand yojanas above [the first].
This second tier extends eight thousand yojanas outward and is composed of the four precious substances;
the Mālādhāra devas dwell therein.
The third tier is ten thousand yojanas above [the second].
This third tier extends four thousand yojanas outward and is composed of the four precious substances;
the gods known as the Constantly Joyful (Sadāmada) dwell therein.
The fourth tier is ten thousand yojanas above [the third].
This fourth tier extends outward by two thousand yojanas and is composed of the four precious substances;
there, the Four Great Kings reside.

The Dharma Master, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa and Subject Shi Hu, and others, respectfully translated by imperial decree:
"Furthermore, Great King!

Above that is the dwelling place of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. There dwell nāga kings upon the waters, namely: Nanda Nāgarāja, Upananda Nāgarāja, Aśvatara Nāgarāja, Mukilinda Nāgarāja, Mānasa Nāgarāja, Elāpattra Nāgarāja, and others. Their lifespans endure for kalpas as they protect and sustain the world, their power being invincible."
These dragon kings, together with the Karoṭapāṇi devas, the Mālādhāra devas, the Sadāmada devas, and the Cāturmahārājika devas, jointly serve as guardians of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.
When the asuras came to engage in battle, they immediately confronted their enemies and raised a great alarm.
At that time, King Mūrdhaja was about to advance further when he was stopped by the dragon kings, who led and protected his army.
The king then asked,
"Why do you not advance?
At that time, the deity in charge of the army replied:
"O Son of Heaven!
This is the Dragon King obstructing the military host.
The king said:
"Furthermore, the dragon kings belong to the class of animals; they are no match for me, yet I have now driven them all to serve as my guides and attendants.
Having spoken these words, the dragons immediately led the king forward to the abode of the Heavenly King Dṛḍhaśiras.
That celestial king asked,
"For what reason have you all come here in such haste?
The nāgas replied:
"A human king named Mūrdhaja is coming here; therefore, I am leading the way.
Then, the Deva King Dṛḍhaśiras immediately halted him and forbade him from proceeding further.
The king then asked,
"Why do you not advance?
The deity presiding over the army replied:
“O Son of Heaven!
Here is the Deva King Dṛḍhaśiras, who has halted his host.
The King said:
"Let this Deva Dṛḍhaśiras also serve as my guide and escort.
Having spoken thus, that deva immediately led the king forward to the presence of the Heavenly King Mālyadhara.
That Heavenly King asked:
"For what reason have you now come here in such haste?
The Heavenly King replied:
"A king named Mūrdhaja shall come here; therefore, I am leading the way.
At that time, the Heavenly King Mālyadhāra immediately stopped him again, not allowing him to proceed further.
The King then asked,
"Why do you not advance?
The deity presiding over the army replied:
“O Devaputra!
Here is the Heavenly King Mālyadhara, who is repelling the host of soldiers.
The king said:
"Let this Mālādhara deva also serve as my guide and escort.
Having spoken thus, that deva immediately led the king forward to the abode of the deva King Nityapramoda.
That heavenly king asked,
"For what reason have you now come here in such haste?
The heavenly king replied:
"A human king named Śikhaṇḍin is coming this way; therefore, I have come forward to guide him.
Then the Deva King Mahādyuti immediately stopped him again, forbidding him from proceeding further.
The king then asked,
"Why do you not advance?
The deity presiding over the army replied:
"O Son of Heaven!
Here is the Heavenly King Constantly Arrogant (Nitya-māna), who has halted his host.
The King said:
"Let this ever-arrogant deva also serve as my guide and escort.
Having spoken these words, that deva immediately led the king forward to the abode of the Four Great Heavenly Kings.
That celestial king asked,
"For what reason have you now come here in such haste?
The celestial king replied:
"There is a king among humans named Mūrdhaja; he is coming here, and therefore I am leading the way.
At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings deliberated with one another, saying, "This king of humans possesses great merit and virtue and has a great reputation; how could we possibly oppose him?"
Having spoken thus, they went together to the abode of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and related the aforementioned matter in full.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, said:
"This one possesses great merit and great renown; I, too, ought not to act in opposition to him."
Having spoken thus, he immediately took a wondrous *argha* vessel and rose forward to welcome him.
At that time, King Mūrdhaja saw from afar the forests upon Mount Sumeru, lush and verdant, as dense as clouds, towering and deep blue, their forms and colors exceptionally beautiful;
he then asked the yakṣa guide Nairvāṇika:
"What is the name of this grove of trees ahead? Nimi replied,
"O Devānām Indra!"

This is the Pārijātaka tree and the Kovidāra trees among the Trāyastriṃśa gods; during the four months of summer, the hosts of those devas enjoy themselves beneath them, sporting at will with the five objects of sensual pleasure.
"O Son of Heaven!
Even now, by going there, one likewise experiences this joy.
When the king heard this, he said to his ministers and assistants:
“Did you all previously see the forest, dark blue like a mass of clouds?
The ministers and attendants replied,
“Indeed, we have seen it.”
The King said:

"These are the Pārijātaka and Kovidāra trees among the Trāyastriṃśa gods. During the four months of summer, those hosts of devas enjoy themselves at will beneath those trees, sporting with the five objects of desire;
you too shall go there and receive such pleasures."
Then King Mūrdhaja proceeded further forward and saw white clouds rising high upon Mount Sumeru, clustered like mountain peaks. He again asked Nīvara:
"What is the name of those white clouds ahead, which cluster like high peaks?"
Nandika replied: "O Devaputra!

This is the Hall of Good Dharma within the Heaven of the Thirty-three. There, the assembly of devas and the Four Great Kings constantly gather to contemplate, examine, and weigh all matters pertaining to the world, whether concerning devas or humans."
"O Son of Heaven!
Now is the time to go there.
Having heard this, the king spoke to his ministers and assistants:
"Did you all previously see white clouds rising high and gathering like mountain peaks?
The ministers and attendants replied,
"Indeed, we have seen them."
The King said:

"This is the Hall of Good Dharma within the Heaven of the Thirty-three. There, the hosts of devas and the Four Great Heavenly Kings constantly assemble to contemplate, observe, and weigh all matters pertaining to the world, whether celestial or human;
you should now proceed there."

At every location, there are *kalpavṛkṣa* (wish-fulfilling) trees of four colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—which produce exquisite garments of these four colors.
Furthermore, there are various trees of exquisite music, namely those that produce flutes, pipes, lutes, harps, and so forth.
There are also various trees of exquisite adornment; from those trees emerge bracelets, anklets, and all manner of fine articles for bodily ornamentation.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of *sudhā* flavored food— namely, blue, yellow, red, and white—
which arrive of their own accord as soon as those deva males and females give rise to the thought of them, according to whatever they desire.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of beverages to be drunk, namely: madhupāna, modakapāna, kātanmālīpāna, and pānaka, etc.

Furthermore, there were various exquisite and magnificent halls and towers, wherein hosts of celestial maidens either sat in peaceful repose or moved about in observation; all of them possessed various kinds of litters, carriages, garments, and ornaments for adornment.
The celestial maidens thronged together, beating drums and performing songs, burning various famous incenses, and providing an abundance of food and drink.
Thus, those celestial hosts and their retinues engaged in playful entertainment, experiencing these superior fruits according to the power of their own merit.
The roads within the garden are twenty yojanas long and half a yojana wide; they are pure and magnificently adorned, with golden sand spread upon the ground.
Everywhere they are sprinkled with sandalwood-scented water, and encircled by golden cords from which hang golden bells.
On both sides of the road, there were likewise various groves of flowering and fruit-bearing trees, where birds frolicked and emitted exquisite melodies;
there were also four-colored *kalpavṛkṣa* (wish-fulfilling) garments trees, music trees, and adornment trees;
furthermore, there were four kinds of ornate carriages, namely: elephant vehicles, horse vehicles, chariot vehicles, and precious litters.

If those celestial males and females intend to ride upon their vehicles to go forth for recreation, as soon as the thought arises, the vehicle arrives according to their wish; having mounted it, they travel about and experience various pleasures.
"Why is this grove named 'Jewel Chariot'?
It is because all the ponds, flowers, fruits, forests, garments, ornaments, and celestial maidens within this grove are adorned with various jewels;
furthermore, because hosts of devaputras ride upon jewel chariots to sport and play therein, for these reasons it is called the Jewel Chariot Grove."

"Furthermore, twenty yojanas to the east of the Ratnavimāna Garden is a ground adorned with jewels, measuring exactly two hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth, and one thousand yojanas in circumference;
it is decorated with one hundred and one kinds of colorful paintings, is pure and soft,
and in its center there are four jeweled terraces interspersed and arrayed as ornaments."
Celestial māndārava flowers were strewn across the ground;
the road was twenty yojanas long and half a yojana wide, pure and magnificently adorned.
It was fully endowed with every kind of tree—those bearing flowers and fruits, those of forest groves, those yielding garments, those producing music, and those providing ornaments.
There are also palanquins that arrive as soon as they are thought of, whereby they enjoy various pleasures.
Therein dwell celestial sages who practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

Furthermore, twenty *yojanas* south of the city of Sudarśana is a park named Kharjūra, exactly two hundred and fifty *yojanas* in length and breadth, with a circumference of one thousand *yojanas*; it is magnificent and exquisite both inside and out, most wonderful and beautiful to behold.
The garden has a golden wall one yojana high;
atop this golden wall are four battlements made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal;
furthermore, there is a surrounding wall leading to the pathways, likewise fashioned from the four precious substances.
The ground within that garden was adorned with one hundred and one kinds of colorful paintings;
furthermore, it was as soft as tūla-cotton and like exquisite fine cloth, sinking when the foot was set down and rising when the foot was lifted.
Celestial *mandārava* flowers are strewn upon the ground there, reaching as deep as the knee; from time to time, a fragrant breeze blows away the withered blossoms and rains down fresh ones.

Within the Coarse and Hard Garden (*Audārika-dṛḍha-udyāna*) is a great pond, fifty *yojanas* in length and breadth and two hundred *yojanas* in circumference; its bottom is paved with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
On the four sides of the pond are four stairways, constructed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.

Within that pond are four jeweled terraces, adorned with an intermingling of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. If the terrace is made of gold, the pillars and beams are made of silver; if the terrace is made of silver, the pillars and beams are made of gold; if the terrace is made of lapis lazuli, the pillars and beams are made of crystal;

and if the terrace is made of crystal, the pillars and beams are made of lapis lazuli. The pool is filled with water that is cool and sweet. Its interior is completely covered with *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses.
Furthermore, various kinds of water-birds sport within the pond, emitting wondrous sounds—namely, lofty and distant sounds, pleasing sounds, and exquisite sounds.

Furthermore, there are various kinds of flowering trees and fruit trees that grow straight and stand upright, perfectly circular and without any deficiency, just as a master garland-maker takes exquisite threads and skillfully arranges, winds, and knots them to form a garland; the groves of flowering and fruit trees are exactly like this.
Upon those trees dwell various kinds of flying birds that emit exquisite sounds as they rest there.
At every location, there are *kalpavṛkṣa* (wish-fulfilling) trees of four colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—from which emerge exquisite garments of these four colors.
Furthermore, there are various trees of wonderful music, namely those that produce the sounds of the *xiāo*, flute, lute (*qín*), harp (*kōnghóu*), and so forth.
Furthermore, there are various trees of exquisite adornment, from which emerge bracelets, anklets, and other fine articles for bodily ornamentation;
there are also four-colored *sodā* foods, namely blue, yellow, red, and white.
Whatever those celestial males and females may desire, it arrives of its own accord the very moment they give rise to the thought.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of beverages to be drunk, namely: madhūka juice, mārdvīka juice, karkandhu juice, and pānaka juice.

Furthermore, there were various exquisite and magnificent halls and pavilions, within which the celestial maidens either sat in peaceful repose or moved about as they gazed upon their surroundings. All possessed diverse types of palanquins, vehicles, garments, and ornaments; the celestial maidens crowded together, beating drums and singing songs, burning various famous incenses and providing an abundance of food and drink.
Those celestial hosts, together with their retinues, sport and enjoy themselves, receiving these superior fruits according to the power of their own merit.
Within the park, the roads are twenty yojanas long and half a yojana wide; they are pure and magnificently adorned, with golden sand strewn upon the ground.
Everywhere, sandalwood-scented water is sprinkled, and golden cords crisscross, from which golden bells hang.
On both sides of the road there were also various groves of flowering and fruit-bearing trees, where birds played and emitted wondrous sounds;
there were also four-colored *kalpavṛkṣa* (wish-fulfilling) clothing trees, music trees, and ornamentation trees;
furthermore, there were four kinds of ornate carriages, namely: elephant vehicles, horse vehicles, chariot vehicles, and precious litters.

If those celestial males and females intend to mount their vehicles to go forth for recreation, as soon as the thought arises, the vehicle arrives according to their wish; having mounted it, they travel about and experience various pleasures.
"Why is this grove named Rough and Hard (Kharasvabhāva)?
It is because all the ponds, flowers, fruits, groves, garments, ornaments, and celestial maidens within this grove are entirely coarse and hard;

furthermore, because the assembly of devaputras in this grove—both in body and mind—are entirely coarse and fierce and delight in combat, it is for these reasons that it is called the Rough and Hard Grove."

Translated by the Dharma Master, the Imperially Ennobled Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Shi-hu and others, by imperial decree:

"Furthermore, twenty yojanas south of the Garden of Coarse Solidity (Kharasāra) lies the Ground of Coarse Solidity. It is exactly two hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth, with a circumference of one thousand yojanas. It is adorned with a hundred and one kinds of variegated paintings, and is pure and soft.
In the center of that ground, four jeweled terraces are interspersed and arrayed as ornaments; celestial *mandārava* flowers are strewn across the earth."

The road is twenty yojanas long and half a yojana wide; it is pure and magnificently adorned, fully endowed with every kind of tree—those bearing flowers and fruits, those of forest groves, those yielding garments, those producing music, and those providing ornaments.
There are also palanquins that arrive as soon as one thinks of them, whereby one experiences all manner of delights.
There, celestial seers practice the holy life.
Furthermore, Sudarśana!

Twenty yojanas to the west of the city is a garden named Citraratha, measuring exactly two hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth, with a circumference of one thousand yojanas; it is magnificent and exquisite both inside and out, most wonderful and beautiful to behold.
The garden has a golden wall one yojana high;
atop this golden wall are four battlements made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal;
furthermore, there is a double wall surrounding the pathways, likewise constructed from the four precious substances.

The ground within that garden was adorned with one hundred and one kinds of colorful paintings; furthermore, it was as soft as *tūla* cotton and like exquisite fine cloth, sinking when the foot was set down and rising when the foot was lifted.
Celestial māndārava flowers are strewn upon the ground to a depth of one’s knee; from time to time, a fragrant breeze blows away the withered blossoms and rains down fresh ones.
Within the Miśrakāvana Garden there is a great pond, fifty yojanas in length and breadth and two hundred yojanas in circumference; its bottom is paved with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
On the four sides of the pond are four stairways, constructed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.

Within that pond were four jeweled terraces, adorned with an intermingling of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. If the terrace was made of gold, the pillars and beams were made of silver; if the terrace was made of silver, the pillars and beams were made of gold; if the terrace was made of lapis lazuli, the pillars and beams were made of crystal; and if the terrace was made of crystal, the pillars and beams were made of lapis lazuli.
The pool was filled with cool and sweet water, and its interior was completely covered with *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses.
Furthermore, there were various kinds of water birds sporting in the ponds, emitting wondrous sounds—namely, lofty and distant sounds, pleasing sounds, and beautiful, exquisite sounds.
Furthermore, there are various kinds of flowering trees and fruit trees that grow straight, stand upright, and are perfectly round without any deficiency;
they are like a master garland-maker who takes exquisite threads and skillfully arranges, twists, and binds them into a garland—the groves of flowering and fruit trees are just like this.
Upon those trees dwell various kinds of flying birds that emit wondrous sounds.
Everywhere there are *kalpavṛkṣa* trees of four colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—from which emerge exquisite garments of those four colors.
There are also various trees of wonderful music, namely flutes, pipes, lutes, harps, and so forth;
and there are various trees of exquisite adornments, from which emerge bracelets, anklets, and all manner of fine articles for bodily ornamentation.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of sudhā-flavored food—namely, blue, yellow, red, and white.
Whenever those deva males and females think of them, they arrive of their own accord the very moment such a thought arises.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of beverages to be drunk, namely: madhupāna, modakapāna, khaṇḍamallikāpāna, and pānakapāna.

Furthermore, there were various exquisite and magnificent halls and pavilions, wherein the celestial maidens either sat in peaceful repose or moved about observing their surroundings. All possessed diverse types of palanquins, carriages, clothing, and ornaments; the celestial maidens crowded together, beating drums and singing songs, burning various famous incenses and providing an abundance of food and drink.
Those celestial hosts, together with their retinues, sport and enjoy themselves, experiencing these superior fruits according to the power of their own merit.
"The roads within the garden are twenty yojanas long and half a yojana wide; they are pure and magnificently adorned, with golden sand strewn upon the ground;
everywhere, sandalwood-scented water is sprinkled."
Golden cords crisscrossed and draped with golden bells;
on both sides of the roads were various groves of flowering and fruit-bearing trees, where birds frolicked and emitted wondrous songs;
there were also four-colored *kalpavṛkṣa* garments-trees, music-trees, and ornament-trees.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of ornate carriages, namely: elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, chariot-vehicles, and precious palanquins.

Whenever those celestial males and females intend to ride them to go forth for recreation, as soon as the thought arises, the vehicles arrive according to their wish; having mounted them, they travel about and experience various pleasures.
"Why is this grove named 'Various Kinds' (Caitraratha)?
It is because all the ponds, flowers, fruits, forests, garments, ornaments, and celestial maidens within this grove are of various kinds;
furthermore, the hosts of devaputras in this grove engage in play and amusement with various types of things. For these reasons, it is called the Grove of Various Kinds."

"Furthermore, twenty yojanas to the west of the Caitraratha Grove lies the Caitraratha ground, exactly two hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth, with a circumference of one thousand yojanas. It is adorned with a hundred and one kinds of colorful paintings, and is pure, soft, and supple.
In the center of that ground, there are four jeweled terraces interspersed and magnificently decorated;
celestial mandārava flowers are strewn across the earth."
The road was twenty yojanas long and half a yojana wide, pure and magnificently adorned;
it was fully endowed with trees bearing flowers and fruits, groves, garments, music, and trees for adornment, each one complete;
there were also palanquins that arrived as soon as they were thought of, whereby they experienced every kind of pleasure.
There, celestial seers practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

Furthermore, twenty *yojanas* north of the city of Sudarśana is a park named Nandana, exactly two hundred and fifty *yojanas* in length and breadth, with a circumference of one thousand *yojanas*. It is adorned both inside and out with exquisite and wondrous beauty;
the park has golden walls one *yojana* high.
Upon the golden wall are four battlements made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal;
there is also a double wall leading to the pathways, likewise fashioned from the four precious substances.

The ground within that garden was adorned with one hundred and one kinds of colorful paintings; furthermore, it was as soft as *tūla* cotton or exquisite fine cloth, sinking when the foot was set down and rising as soon as the foot was lifted.

Celestial *mandārava* flowers were strewn across the ground to a depth of a knee’s length; whenever a fragrant breeze blew, it carried away the withered blossoms and rained down fresh ones in their place.
"In the Nandana Grove there is a great pond, fifty yojanas in length and breadth and two hundred yojanas in circumference;
its bottom is paved with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. On the four sides of the pond are four stairways made of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.

Within that pond are four jeweled pavilions, adorned with an intermingling of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal: if the pavilion is made of gold, the pillars and beams are made of silver; if the pavilion is made of silver, the pillars and beams are made of gold; if the pavilion is made of lapis lazuli, the pillars and beams are made of crystal; and if the pavilion is made of crystal, the pillars and beams are made of lapis lazuli."
The pool is filled with clear, cool, sweet water;
it is completely covered within by *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers.
Furthermore, various kinds of aquatic birds sport within the pool, emitting exquisite sounds—namely, lofty sounds, pleasing sounds, and beautiful sounds.
Furthermore, there are various kinds of flowering trees and fruit trees that grow straight up, standing upright and perfectly circular without any deficiency;
they are just like a master garland-maker who takes exquisite thread and skillfully arranges, twists, and binds it into a garland—the groves of flowering and fruit trees are exactly like this.
Upon those trees dwell various kinds of flying birds that emit wondrous sounds;
everywhere there are *kalpavṛkṣa* trees of four colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—from which issue exquisite garments of those four colors;
furthermore, there are various trees of wonderful music, namely flutes, pipes, lutes, harps, and so forth.
Furthermore, there are various trees of exquisite adornment, from which emerge bracelets for the hands, anklets for the feet, and all manner of fine ornaments for the body.
There are also four-colored foods of *sodāsa* flavor— namely, blue, yellow, red, and white— which,
whether for those celestial males or celestial females, arrive of their own accord as soon as the thought arises.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of beverages to be drunk, namely: *madhūka* juice, *mṛdvīkā* juice, *karkaṭaka* juice, and *pāna* juice, among others.
Furthermore, there were various exquisite and wondrously adorned palaces and towers, wherein the celestial maidens either sat in peaceful repose or looked out while strolling about.

All possessed diverse types of litters, carriages, garments, and ornaments; the celestial maidens gathered in great numbers, beating drums and singing songs, burning various famous incenses, and providing an abundance of food and drink.
Those celestial beings and their retinues sport and enjoy themselves, experiencing these superior fruits according to the power of their own merit.

The roads within the grove are twenty yojanas long and half a yojana wide; they are pure and magnificently adorned, with golden sand strewn upon the ground, and everywhere sprinkled with sandalwood-scented perfumed water.
Golden cords crisscrossed and hung with golden bells;
on both sides of the roads were various groves of flowering and fruit-bearing trees, where birds frolicked and emitted exquisite melodies;
there were also four-colored *kalpavṛkṣa* (wish-fulfilling) garment trees, music trees, and ornamentation trees.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of ornate carriages: namely, elephant-vehicles, horse-vehicles, chariot-vehicles, and precious litters.

When those deva males and deva females intend to ride them to go for recreation, as soon as the thought arises, they arrive in accordance with that thought; having mounted them, they travel about and experience various pleasures.
"Why is this grove named 'Joyful' (Nandana)?

It is because all the ponds, flowers, fruits, groves, garments, ornaments, and celestial maidens within it are enjoyed by those hosts of devas for their play and amusement; according to the power of their own merit, their minds give rise to satisfaction, joy, and happiness.
For these reasons, it is called the Joyful Grove."

"Furthermore, twenty yojanas to the north of the Nandana Grove is the Nandana Ground, measuring exactly two hundred and fifty yojanas in length and breadth, with a circumference of one thousand yojanas. It is adorned with a hundred and one kinds of variegated paintings, pure and soft;
in the center of that ground are four jeweled terraces interspersed and arrayed as ornaments;
and celestial māndārava flowers are strewn across its surface."
The road is twenty yojanas long and half a yojana wide, pure and magnificently adorned;
it is fully provided with every kind of tree bearing flowers and fruits, as well as trees yielding garments, music, and ornaments;
there are also palanquins that arrive the moment one thinks of them, whereby one experiences all manner of delights.
There, celestial seers practice the holy life.
Furthermore, to the northeast of the city of Sudarśana, there is a tree named Pārijātaka-kovidāra.
The roots of that tree spread fifty yojanas; each branch extends fifty yojanas.

Its first branch extends fifty yojanas to the east, the second branch fifty yojanas to the south, the third branch fifty yojanas to the west, and the fourth branch fifty yojanas to the north; the central branch rises high into the void for fifty yojanas.
That tree is one hundred and fifty yojanas in height, fifty yojanas in diameter, and three hundred yojanas in circumference.
Its exquisite fragrance is perceived for one hundred yojanas with the wind and fifty yojanas against the wind;
its color and radiance illuminate eighty yojanas;
and its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits bloom and fall according to their proper seasons.

Whenever the hosts of the Trāyastriṃśa devas behold this tree at the time of its half-blossomed *puṇḍarīka* flowers, their hearts are filled with joy, and those celestial hosts roam about in play and delight.
Before long, those trees again became *śirīṣa-prapuṇḍarīkas*;
the hosts of devas felt joy in their hearts and wandered about in play and delight.
Before long, those trees again became *jālaka-jāta*.
Those hosts of devas felt joy arise in their hearts as they wandered about in play and delight.
Before long, those trees again appeared as *cāru-karaja-druma*;
those hosts of devas felt joy arise in their hearts as they wandered about in play and delight.
Before long, those trees vanished, and the bone-pressing Mālukyāntaka was seen again;
the hosts of devas felt joy in their hearts as they wandered about in play and delight.
Before long, they again see the *kakkāsa-kañjāta* tree;
the hosts of devas feel joy in their hearts and wander about in play and delight.
Before long, they again see it in full, fragrant bloom, spreading everywhere.
When those hosts of devas see that the Pārijātaka-kovidāra tree has blossomed in full bloom, their hearts are filled with joy;
for four months of summer, they enjoy the pleasures of the five senses beneath its shade, sporting with sovereign ease, experiencing such superior fruits according to the power of their own merit.
The Buddha said,
"Great King!
By the power of merit, the excellence of the Pārijātaka-kovidāra tree among those gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven is such as this."

Furthermore, beneath the Pārijātaka and Kovidāra trees of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven lies a variegated ground, fifty yojanas square and two hundred yojanas in circumference, exquisite and beautiful to behold.

It is adorned with one hundred and one kinds of colorful patterns; it is pure and soft like tūla-cotton or fine karpāsa cloth, sinking when the foot is set down and rising as soon as the foot is lifted.
Heavenly māndārava flowers are strewn across its surface, and from time to time a fragrant breeze blows away the withered blossoms and rains down fresh ones.
Within it was spread a most excellent and noble seat made of pure gold, upon which Śakra, Lord of the Devas, sat;
there the host of devaputras of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven dwelt and moved about during the four months of summer, enjoying themselves with the five desires and sporting at their own will.

Furthermore, the ground was adorned all around with soft and variegated decorations. There were also various kinds of flowering trees and fruit-bearing trees that grew straight, stood upright, and were perfectly circular without any deficiency, just as a master garland-maker takes exquisite threads and skillfully arranges, coils, and knots them into a garland; the groves of flowering and fruiting trees were likewise so.
Various birds perched and moved upon them, emitting wonderful sounds.
There were also four-colored *kalpavṛkṣa* (wish-fulfilling) trees, from which exquisite garments of four colors emerged.
Furthermore, there are various trees of exquisite music, namely those that produce flutes, pipes, lutes, harps, and so forth;
there are also various trees of exquisite adornment, from which emerge bracelets, anklets, and all manner of fine articles for bodily ornamentation;
and there are foods of the *sudhā* flavor in four colors: blue, yellow, red, and white.
Whatever those celestial males and females may think of, it all arrives of its own accord.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of beverages to be drunk, namely: madhūpāna, mādhvīka, kṣaudra, and pānaka.

Furthermore, there were various exquisite and magnificent palaces and towers where celestial maidens sat in peaceful repose or wandered about observing their surroundings. They all possessed diverse types of litters, carriages, clothing, and ornaments; the celestial maidens gathered in great numbers, beating drums and singing songs, burning various famous incenses, and providing an abundance of food and drink.

Then those celestial hosts, together with their retinues, for the four months of summer, enjoy themselves at will with the pleasures of the five senses, experiencing these superior fruits according to the power of their own merit.
