Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao Feng Da Fu, Acting Guang... [Title] of the Great Song Dynasty.
Translated by the Imperial Decree by the Dharma Master Shihu, Grand Minister of Remuneration, recipient of the purple robe, and śramaṇa, together with others:
"Furthermore, in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, there is a great elephant king named Airāvaṇa, who guards the gardens and groves."
His physical form was worthy of contemplation, being purely white in color like a kumuda flower, with seven limbs touching the ground;
the head of this elephant king was most excellent and beautiful, red within and blue without like the color of indranīla, and he possessed six tusks;
his body was two and a half yojanas long, one yojana wide from front to back, seven yojanas in circumference, and one and a half yojanas high.
Furthermore, that elephant king had eight thousand elephants as his retinue;

their bodies were all white like kumuda flowers, with seven limbs touching the ground, and each elephant’s head was endowed with perfect color and form, resembling sapphire, and each possessed six tusks.

When those hosts of devas desire to go out for recreation and to enjoy the various gardens, the beloved elephant king Airāvaṇa, knowing the time and responding to their wish, manifests thirty-two heads through his supernormal power. Each head has six tusks; upon each tusk are seven times seven ponds; in each pond are seven times seven lotuses; within each flower are seven times seven pedestals; within each pedestal are seven times seven pavilions; within each pavilion are seven times seven guards; each guard has seven times seven celestial maidens (apsarases); each maiden has seven times seven handmaidens; and each handmaiden strikes seven times seven celestial drums. As for the most excellent head of the elephant king, Śakra mounts it.
The thirty-two devas were stationed respectively upon the heads of those beings they had transformed, while the remaining hosts of devas dwelt there according to their respective positions;
when the Elephant King moved, he was as swift as a whirlwind, such that neither the celestial sons nor the celestial daughters could perceive his front or rear.
Furthermore, the elephant king Airāvaṇa carries the assembly of devas as they travel throughout the Heaven of the Thirty-three, proceeding from each city to each garden.
By the power of their supernormal transformations, they all assume forms identical to those of the devaputras and devīs in terms of their supernormal powers and majestic majesty;

together with that assembly of devas, they enjoy the pleasures of the five desires and sport with sovereign ease, receiving these superior fruits in accordance with the power of their respective merits.
The Buddha said,
"Great King!
Such is the power of Airāvaṇa, the king of elephants, who guards the gardens and groves within that Heaven of the Thirty-three."

"Furthermore, to the southwest of the celestial city of Sudarśana, there is the Sudharmā Hall. It is three hundred yojanas long, three hundred yojanas wide, nine hundred yojanas in circumference, and three hundred and fifty yojanas high; it is magnificent and beautiful to behold."
The Hall of Good Dharma has crystal for its floor; its pavilions, staircases, and steps are likewise composed of crystal.

There are four jeweled terraces, adorned with the alternating intermingling of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal: if the terrace is made of gold, the pillars and beams are made of silver; if the terrace is made of silver, the pillars and beams are made of gold; if the terrace is made of lapis lazuli, the pillars and beams are made of crystal; and if the terrace is made of crystal, the pillars and beams are made of lapis lazuli.
Furthermore, the road circling the Sudharmā Hall is pure and magnificently adorned, with golden sand strewn upon the ground;
everywhere it is sprinkled with sandalwood-scented water,
and golden cords crisscross, from which hang golden bells to mark the edges of the path.

Furthermore, there are various kinds of flowering trees and fruit trees that grow straight, stand upright, and are perfectly circular without any deficiency, just as a master garland-maker takes exquisite threads and skillfully arranges, winds, and knots them to form a garland; the groves of flowering and fruit trees are exactly like this.
Upon those trees, various kinds of birds alight and dwell, emitting exquisite sounds;
furthermore, there are *kalpavṛkṣa* trees of four colors—blue, yellow, red, and white—from which emerge exquisite garments of those four colors;
and there are various trees of wonderful music, namely flutes, pipes, lutes, harps, and so forth.
Furthermore, there are various trees of exquisite adornment, from which emerge bracelets, anklets, and other fine articles for bodily ornamentation.
There are also four-colored *sodā* foods, namely blue, yellow, red, and white;
and there are four kinds of sweet nectars, namely *madhuka* nectar, *mṛdvīkā* nectar, *khaṇḍamṛdvīkā* nectar, and *pāna* nectar, among others.
Whatever those celestial males and female deities may desire arrives of its own accord the very moment they conceive the thought.

Furthermore, there are various exquisite and magnificent palaces and towers; within them, the hosts of celestial maidens sit in peaceful repose or wander about in observation. They all possess various types of carriages, vehicles, garments, and ornaments. The celestial maidens crowd together, beating drums and singing songs, burning various famous incenses and providing an abundance of food and drink.
Those celestial hosts, together with their retinues, sport and enjoy themselves, experiencing such superior fruits according to the power of their own merit.
Furthermore, beside the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā), there are seven flowing channels, each one yojana in depth and breadth; their bottoms are paved with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
On all four sides of these channels are four stairways, likewise composed of the four precious substances.

And there were four jeweled terraces, adorned with an intermingling of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal. Where the terrace was made of gold, the pillars and beams were made of silver; where the terrace was made of silver, the pillars and beams were made of gold; where the terrace was made of lapis lazuli, the pillars and beams were made of crystal; and where the terrace was made of crystal, the pillars and beams were made of lapis lazuli.
The water in those channels was cool, sweet, and filled them to the brim;
blue lotuses (*utpala*), red lotuses (*padma*), white lotuses (*kumuda*), and yellow lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*) were spread throughout their interior.
Furthermore, there were various water-birds sporting about and emitting exquisite sounds;
flowers, fruits, groves, garments, music, and trees for adornment were each fully present;
within these seven channels, there were also various exceptionally beautiful pavilions and terraces.
Those hosts of devas sport and enjoy themselves in happiness.

Furthermore, the gate of the Sudharmā Hall is lofty and magnificent; above it is a multi-storied pavilion with staircases arranged on its sides, exquisitely adorned. Each staircase has sixteen pillars, and there are seven tiers of roads arranged in a continuous circuit.
Beside these roads are octagonal pillars made of lapis lazuli, pure and beautiful, upon which are spread subtle pavilions the size of a hair-tip that do not touch or obstruct one another.
In the Sudharmā Hall there was a most excellent and noble seat made of pure gold;
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, sat upon it, while the other celestial hosts were assigned seats in order, with the seat for King Mūrdhaja arranged at the very end.
"At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with the hosts of devas, holding *argha* vases, rose and went forward to welcome King Mūrdhaja.
Then the majestically powerful King Mūrdhaja entered in due order, while his other attendants each took their places outside."
The king then reflected:
"Should I, too, now occupy this seat?
He further thought:
"How wonderful it would be if Lord Śakra, King of Devas, were to offer me half his seat and invite me to sit together with him!
The Buddha said,
"Great King!..."
When King Mūrdhagata had this thought, Śakra immediately knew it and offered him half of his seat, inviting him to sit together.

At that time, as King Mūrdhagata shared the seat with Śakra, Lord of Devas, there was no difference between them in the size or features of their bodies, in their deportment or majestic radiance, in their voices or speech, nor in their ornaments;
the only distinction was that the king’s blinking of his eyes differed from that of the Lord of Devas.
The Buddha said,
"Great King! That King Mandhātu resided in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, and in this manner, six Indras passed away."
"Furthermore, at a later time, the hosts of the Trāyastriṃśa gods engage in battle with the asuras;
if the asura forces are defeated, they immediately enter their own palaces, bolt the doors, and remain hidden within;
if the gods are defeated, they likewise enter the celestial palaces, bolt the doors, and remain hidden within."

"Furthermore, among the Trāyastriṃśa gods there is another elephant king named Supratiṣṭhita. His physical form is magnificent to behold; he is pure white in color like a kumuda flower, and his seven limbs rest upon the ground.
The elephant king’s head is red on the inside and blue on the outside, like the color of an indranīla gem.
He possesses six tusks, and his body is two and a half yojanas long. His width from front to back is one yojana each, his circumference is seven yojanas, and he is one and a half yojanas high."

He has eight thousand elephants as his retinue; their bodies are all white like *kumuda* flowers, with seven limbs touching the ground, and each elephant’s head is endowed with perfect color and form;
they are also like sapphire in hue, and each possesses six tusks.
During the four months of winter, that noble elephant king, Supratiṣṭhita, dwells together with his retinue in a place adjacent to where the asuras reside.
Furthermore, twenty yojanas to the north of Mount Gandhamādana, near the dwelling place of the asuras, there is a high mound;
it is fifty yojanas in length and breadth, two hundred yojanas in circumference, and three and a half yojanas in height, composed entirely of pure gold.

The ground was magnificently adorned and strewn with golden sand; everywhere it was sprinkled with sandalwood-scented water, and crisscrossed by golden cords from which hung golden bells and chimes. Thorny brambles and gravel were naturally cleared away.
On its four sides there were furthermore eight thousand small hills, also composed of gold;

their grounds were likewise strewn with golden sand, sprinkled everywhere with sandalwood-scented water, crisscrossed by golden cords from which hung golden bells and chimes, and naturally free of thorny brambles and gravel.
The road therein was twenty yojanas long and one and a half yojanas wide; it was entirely pure, magnificent, and beautiful to behold.

Whenever the elephant king Supratiṣṭhita dwelt upon those high elevations during the four months of summer, his retinue of eight thousand elephants would likewise gather around him in succession and remain there, guarding their elephant king in secret.
"Furthermore, twenty yojanas to the south of the high ridge, there is a great king of *śāla* trees named Supratiṣṭhita;
it is surrounded on all sides by seven rows of various *śāla* trees."

The root of that king of trees, the Well-Established (Susthitā), extends fourteen spans; the roots of the first row of trees extend thirteen spans; those of the second row, twelve spans; those of the third row, eleven spans; those of the fourth row measure ten spans; those of the fifth row measure nine spans; those of the sixth row measure eight spans; and those of the seventh row measure seven spans.

The king of trees, well-established with branches and leaves luxuriantly dense, hangs down and covers the first row of trees; the first row of trees in turn hangs down and covers the second row of trees; and so it continues in succession through the third up to the sixth;
the seventh row of trees has branches and leaves spreading wide, rising high into the vast expanse;
the ground is pure, magnificent, and beautiful to behold.
The road therein is twenty yojanas long and one and a half yojanas wide, and it is entirely pure.

Whenever the elephant king Supratiṣṭhita proceeds from his dwelling place to the site of the king of sāla trees, Supratiṣṭhita, he may depart at will in his original form, or by the power of his supernatural majesty, manifesting the appearance of a deva and returning mounted upon a single elephant; or he may ride upon its shoulders or its head, traveling through the air amidst the sounds of natural music and song as he sports along.

Furthermore, whenever the Elephant King dwells beneath the king of trees, his retinue of eight thousand elephants will station themselves facing inward within seven rows of *sāla* trees. Just as the first row of trees stands facing inward, so too do the second, third, and up to the seventh rows stand facing inward, providing the Elephant King with secret protection.
"Furthermore, twenty yojanas to the east of the King of Well-Situated Śāla Trees, there is a great pond named Mandākinī, fifty yojanas in length and breadth and two hundred yojanas in circumference;
it is filled with cool, sweet water,
and its interior is strewn everywhere with *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers."
Water birds frolic about, emitting wondrous sounds—namely, lofty and distant tones, pleasing sounds, and exquisite melodies.

In the ponds, lotuses are as large as chariot wheels; their stalks are as thick as a chariot’s yoke; their petals are exquisite and broad like the dewlap of a bull-king; and their lotus roots are plump and round like the thighs of a man, with a most excellent flavor as sweet as milk.

On all four sides of the pond, there were furthermore eight thousand smaller ponds, all of which were magnificent and beautiful, filled with water, and likewise strewn throughout with exquisite flowers. Water birds frolicked within them, emitting wondrous sounds; the lotuses in the ponds were as large as chariot wheels, their stalks, leaves, and roots all being equally vast.

"Furthermore, the road therein is twenty yojanas long and one and a half yojanas wide; it is magnificent and pure, with golden sand spread upon the ground, everywhere sprinkled with sandalwood-scented water, and crisscrossed by golden cords from which golden bells hang; thorns, brambles, and gravel are naturally removed."

“At that time, when the noble elephant king Supratiṣṭhita departs from the king of śāla trees named Supratiṣṭhita for the Puṇḍarīka pond, he may go there assuming his natural form as he pleases; or, by means of his supernormal powers, manifesting the appearance of a deva or a human, he returns mounted upon a single elephant—either riding upon its shoulder or its head—and proceeds through the air sporting amidst the sounds of music and song.”
Furthermore, when the Elephant King enters that pond to enjoy himself, his retinue of eight thousand elephants also stays there surrounding him, guarding the Elephant King closely.
"Furthermore, after the Elephant King Supratiṣṭhita has enjoyed himself to his heart's content within that pond, he rests upon its bank;

at that time, the foremost among the eight thousand elephants first enters the pond, takes lotus roots and stalks, washes them until they are perfectly clean, and presents them before the Elephant King to provide him with food."
Having eaten their fill and being thoroughly satisfied, the elephant king and his retinue of elephants returned one after another to that pond;
having each played and frolicked to their heart's content, they also took lotus roots and sprouts, washed them clean, and ate them.
The Buddha said,
"Great King!
Such is the majestic power of the Elephant King Supratiṣṭhita belonging to those gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
"Furthermore, thereafter, that asura arrayed his fourfold army— namely, the elephant corps, the cavalry, the chariot corps, and the infantry—
and donned four kinds of sturdy armor, adorned with an intermingling of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal; wielding four kinds of sharp weapons,
namely bows, swords, spears, and blades, he emerged from his own palace seeking to engage in battle with the hosts of the Thirty-three Gods."

At that time, the Dragon King dwelling in the waters saw the asuras arraying their fourfold army, clad in armor and wielding sharp weapons as they emerged from the asura palace seeking battle with the devas.

Having seen this, the Dragon King likewise marshaled his fourfold army, donned armor adorned with the four jewels—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—and, grasping his weapons, engaged in battle with the asuras.
When the Naga King is victorious and the host of Asuras is defeated and retreats, the Asuras immediately enter their own palaces;

when the Asuras are victorious and the Naga King is defeated and retreats, the military forces of the foremost guardians of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven are scattered, and they flee from the great ocean to the first terrace of Sumeru, the King of Mountains, where the Heavenly King Dṛḍhaśiras dwells.
"At that time, the Heavenly King Dṛḍhaśiras, together with the Water-Dwelling Dragon King, joined their forces to wage war against the host of Asuras.
When the two guardians were victorious and the host of Asuras had been defeated and retreated, they would enter their own palaces;

but when the Asuras were victorious and the two guardians were defeated and retreated, the military forces of the two guardians of the Thirty-three Heavens were scattered, and they proceeded from the first terrace of Mount Sumeru to the second terrace, where the Heavenly King Māladhara dwells."
The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of King Mūrdhaja Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Five.
The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of King Mūrdhaja Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao Feng Da Fu, Acting Director of the Bureau of Sacrifices.
Translated by the Imperial Decree by the Dharma Master Shihu, Grand Master of Merit, and the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Shi Hu, et al.:
"At that time, the three guardians—the Heavenly King Mālādhara, the Heavenly King Dṛḍhaśiras, and the Dragon King Jalavāsin—united their strength and fought together against the asuras."
When the Three Guardians are victorious and the host of asuras is defeated, they immediately enter their own palaces;

when the asuras are victorious and the Three Guardians are defeated, the military forces of the Three Guardians of the Thirty-three Heavens are scattered and dispersed, and they proceed from the second terrace of Mount Sumeru to the third terrace, where the Heavenly King Nityapraharsa resides.
"At that time, the Heavenly King Nitya-mada, the Heavenly King Mālādhara, the Heavenly King Dṛḍhaśiras, and the Dragon King Jalavāsin joined their forces and fought together against the asuras."
When the Four Guardians are victorious and the host of asuras is defeated, they immediately enter their own palaces;

when the asuras are victorious and the Four Guardians are defeated, the military forces of the Four Guardians of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven are scattered, and they proceed from the third terrace of Mount Sumeru to the fourth terrace, where the Four Great Heavenly Kings reside.

"At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings—the King of Constant Joy, the King of Holding Garlands, the King of Firm Head, and the Dragon King Dwelling in Water—united their strength and engaged in battle with the asuras."
When the five guardians are victorious and the host of asuras is defeated and retreats, they immediately enter their own palaces;

when the asuras are victorious and the five guardians are defeated and retreat, the military forces of the five guardians of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven are thus broken and scattered, proceeding from the fourth terrace of Mount Sumeru up to the abode of Śakra, Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Finally, when the host of asuras had defeated and scattered the five classes of protective troops, they reorganized their fourfold army and proceeded to the abode of Śakra to seek battle.
"At that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings went to the palace of Śakra; having arrived, they addressed him, saying:
'Lord of Devas!
The hosts of asuras, arrayed with the fourfold army, have come seeking battle, and the five protectors among the gods have been scattered and put to flight.'"
Now they have returned to the abode of the Lord of Devas; their hosts are powerful and superior, and we cannot withstand them.
O Lord of Devas!
At this time, we pray that you grant us the power of battle.
At that time, having heard these words, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the assembly of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, saying:
"O virtuous ones!
You should know that the host of asuras, having broken and scattered our five protectors through their fierce strength in battle, have returned here to seek combat with me."
"O virtuous ones!
Now is the time to exert your heroic strength.
At that moment, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had this thought:
"It is fit for the noble elephant king Supratiṣṭhita to ride and control.

Then, the noble elephant king Supratiṣṭhita, knowing the thought of the Lord of Devas, vanished from his dwelling place in Jambudvīpa and arrived in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm.

He then manifested thirty-two heads; each head had six tusks, and upon each tusk were seven times seven ponds. In each pond were seven times seven lotuses, and within each lotus were seven times seven pedestals. Within each pedestal were seven times seven pavilions, and within each pavilion were seven times seven guardians. Each guardian had seven times seven celestial maidens, and each maiden had seven times seven handmaidens. Each handmaiden struck seven times seven celestial drums, while Śakra mounted the most excellent head of the Elephant King.
The thirty-two devas were stationed upon the heads of the emanated elephant in their respective order, while the remaining hosts of devas dwelt there according to their capacity.
As the Elephant King moved, he was as swift as the turning of the wind; neither the celestial sons nor the celestial daughters could perceive his front or his rear.

When the elephant king Supratiṣṭhita had reached the Heaven of the Thirty-three, he emerged from the southern gate and went to the Caitraratha Garden; there, manifesting the form of a celestial being through his own supernatural power, he sported and enjoyed himself with the hosts of devas.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, mounted the Elephant King and marshaled the fourfold army; all were clad in armor adorned with the four precious jewels and wielded four kinds of sharp and keen weapons, intending to engage in battle with the hosts of asuras.
At that time, King Mūrdhaja, having witnessed these events, addressed Śakra, saying:
"Lord of Devas!
Set aside the matter of battle for now; I wish to compete with him in military strength."
The Lord of Devas replied, "According to your wish; now is precisely the right time.
Then King Mūrdhaja, together with an army of eighteen koṭis of troops of superior strength, ascended into the air, drew his bow, and snapped the string, emitting a swift and piercing sound.
When the host of asuras heard this sound, they asked,
"Whose is the sound of these vibrating strings?
One who knew replied:
"This is the sound of King Māndhātṛ tuning his lute.
At that time, the asuras were struck with wonder;
furthermore, it is the natural law that when the hosts of asuras and devas wage war, their military forces are equal, with neither side gaining any advantage over the other.
As soon as King Mūrdhaja dispatched his armies, his valor and strength were so superior that he ascended into the air and remained there.
At that time, the asuras thought to themselves:

"We have long heard that among the kings of men there is one named Mūrdhaja, a courageous hero endowed with great merit and virtue, whose majestic power is exceptionally honored and peerless, rising high into the void beyond our reach."
Having spoken these words, he was immediately seized by fear and retreated into his own palace.
Then, King Mūrdhaja asked his ministers and officials:
"Among these military forces, which side is victorious?"
The ministers replied,
"Your Majesty has now achieved victory.
The king then reflected:
"And I have surpassed these Trāyastriṃśa gods;
I have ruled over Jambudvīpa, Pūrvavideha, Aparagoyānī, and Uttarakuru;
I am endowed with the seven treasures and possess a thousand sons; I am of supreme physical appearance, courageous and fearless, capable of subduing the armies of others."
Furthermore, within the palace, he rained down gold coins for seven days;
then, ascending to the Heaven of the Thirty-three, he entered the palace of Śakra and took his place upon half the seat in the Sudharmā Hall, saying:
"If the Lord Śakra should pass away from this seat, I shall govern the celestial realm and likewise become a king of men."
"How wonderful it would be to be the most excellent among gods and humans!

As soon as the king gave rise to this thought, his supernormal powers and majestic authority immediately vanished, and he was cast back down into his original palace on Jambudvīpa. Thereupon, illness and affliction arose, pressing upon his body;
moreover, he became so emaciated and exhausted that he approached the brink of death.
At that time, among the ministers and attendants, there was one who was the eldest and most eminent; he approached the king and addressed him, saying:
"O Son of Heaven!
Should someone come at a later time and pose this question:"
"What were the final words spoken by Great King Mūrdhaja when he was approaching the end of his life?
How should one answer this? The king said to him:
"After I have passed away, if someone comes and asks this question, you should answer:
'King Mahāsudarśana was uniquely distinguished by his majesty and virtue; he possessed the seven treasures in their entirety and alone among men possessed the four kinds of supernormal power.'"
What are the four?

The Great King Mūrdhaja attained a long life and dwelt in the world for a period during which one hundred and fourteen Śakras passed away and perished; this is the first supernormal power of longevity.

Furthermore, King Māndhātṛ’s supreme countenance was exceptionally sublime and beautiful to behold; his features surpassed those of humans and were endowed with the marks of a celestial being. This was the second supernormal power of physical appearance.

Furthermore, King Māndhātṛ possessed all requisites for enjoyment; he had little illness and little affliction, his physical strength was robust and healthy, and his digestion was untroubled when consuming various flavors. The seasons were neither too cold nor too hot, being perfectly harmonious, so that whatever he used for sustenance brought him complete peace and happiness. This is the third supernatural power of freedom from disease.
Furthermore, King Mūrdhaja was beloved by all who beheld him; they gazed upon him without weariness, just as a son cherishes his father.

Moreover, the king nurtured and protected his subjects with a heart of joy and affection, like a father loves his children. On one occasion, while the king was traveling through the pleasure gardens for recreation, he said to his charioteer:
"Drive the carriage forward slowly, so that it may proceed at a leisurely pace and allow the people to behold me."
Again, the multitude said to the charioteer:
"O worthy one!
Please drive the carriage slowly so that we may linger and behold the marks and signs of the King's excellence."
"This is the fourth power of delight.
Furthermore, King Māndhātṛ reigned as the supreme sovereign over the four great continents; later, he went to the Heaven of the Thirty-three, where Śakra offered him half of his throne.
Such were his achievements."
Furthermore, he felt no weariness or satisfaction regarding the five desires; as his life was drawing to a close, he spoke this verse:
“Alas! The realm of worldly desire— Though gold and jewels abound, there is no satiety.
In this, pleasure is slight while suffering is vast; The wise should understand this accordingly.”
Even regarding the exquisite sensual pleasures found among the gods, one is not liberated due to the mind of craving and attachment;
who is able to exhaust the source of craving?
Only the Tathāgata and his noble disciples.
Even if one were to accumulate vast quantities of pure gold, equal in measure to Mount Sumeru, no one could ever give rise to a mind of satiety;
the wise person awakens well to this truth.
If one considers desire to be the cause of suffering, why would one feel craving and attachment toward objects of desire?
Greed and the like are the sorrows of the world; the wise should train themselves well in subduing them.
The Buddha said: “Great King!
For these reasons, King Mūrdhagata also spoke thus:”
"Among the people of the world, few are able to awaken to contentment within the objects of the five desires before their lives come to an end;

rather, most people in the world, unable to awaken to such understanding and failing to develop weariness with or satisfaction regarding the objects of the five desires, pass away at the end of their lives."
"Furthermore, King Mūrdhagata, for the sake of extensively benefiting future generations, spoke again in verse:
'Within the most wretched flow of saṃsāra, One clearly perceives that life-span diminishes with each passing moment;
One should swiftly cultivate the various gateways of merit, For not cultivating meritorious deeds is itself suffering.'"
Therefore, cultivate merit as your supreme desire; practice giving according to the proper ritual.
In this world and in the world beyond, joy arises through the cultivation of merit.

At that time, all the people of the kingdom, numbering in the hundreds of thousands, hearing that the king was bedridden with illness, all came running to visit him, gazing upon him and offering their greetings.

At that time, King Mūrdhaja, for the sake of the multitude of people, extensively explained the remedies for various conditions such as craving and desire, so as to cause those people to renounce their homes and study the Path.
At that time, there were countless hundreds of thousands of people who, having heard what was said, all left the household life to cultivate the four brahma-vihāras;
furthermore, many others severed their desire and greed and were reborn in the Brahma-world.
The Buddha said, “Great King!

From the time that King Mūrdhagata first occupied the rank of a youth up until his position as crown prince, and his rule over Jambudvīpa, Pūrvavideha, Aparagodānīya, and Uttarakuru, he held the station of a Wheel-turning Monarch;”
Furthermore, while dwelling upon the seven golden mountains and traveling through various stations as far as the Heaven of the Thirty-three,
a total of one hundred and fourteen Śakras passed away during that interval.

Great King, you should know that regarding the lifespan of Śakra: one hundred human years constitute a single day and night in the Heaven of the Thirty-three; thirty such days and nights make one month, and twelve such months make one year.
A thousand such celestial years is their lifespan. Calculating those thousand years by human standards, it is three koṭis and six million years.
"Furthermore, Great King!
In the past, King Māndhātṛ conceived the thought that Śakra, Lord of the Devas, should share half his throne with him;
at that time, the Bhikṣu Kāśyapa was serving as Śakra."
Furthermore, King Māndhātṛ again had this thought:
"If Śakra, Lord of the Devas, were to pass away from this seat, I would be the sovereign over both heaven and earth; would that not be wonderful!"

At that time, while Kāśyapa Tathāgata served as the Lord Śakra, King Mūrdhaja—who possessed great and supreme merit and a vast reputation—conceived a mental transgression in a single thought; his supernormal powers diminished and he fell back into decline, becoming ensnared by acute affliction before passing away.
The Buddha said,
"Great King!
Could that King Mandhātu have been anyone else?"
I am that very person.

At that time, I extensively bestowed benefit and happiness upon sentient beings and strove toward supreme wisdom; yet, there were many demonic obstacles to my *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, brought about by the power of causes and conditions.
At that time, the Great King Jayasena, the ruler of the kingdom of Kośala, suddenly conceived a doubt and approached the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

During the causal conditions of that King Mūrdhaja in the distant past, what karmic actions did he cultivate to bring about such a result—that there was a natural rain of gold coins within his palace for seven days?"

The Buddha said, “Great King! In the distant past, a Buddha appeared in the world, named Sarvottama Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.”
At that time, there was the son of a householder who, in accordance with the worldly rites, entered into marriage with a young girl in that kingdom.

His wife presented her husband with exquisite flowers made of the four precious gems and sweet food and drink; having accepted them, the husband took these precious flowers and returned home by carriage.
On the way, he beheld the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Sarvābhyudgata, traveling in a measured and dignified manner through the streets.

When the elder’s son beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One, adorned with the thirty-two marks of excellence and sublime beauty, he immediately conceived the highest, pure faith and joy. He descended from his carriage and, with solemn reverence, offered the flowers;

through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, those flowers were instantly transformed to be as large as chariot wheels, circling in the air, sometimes drifting and sometimes coming to rest.
At that time, the son of the elder gave rise to a pure mind and spoke these verses:
"By this cause of vast generosity, may I attain the Buddha’s spontaneous wisdom of the world;
May I swiftly cross the stream of birth and death, and deliver all those not yet delivered by previous Buddhas."
To all the supreme Buddhas, the Great Sages, I offer these pleasing flowers;
by this vast cause, may I fulfill the unsurpassed path I seek.
The Buddha said: "Great King!
For that reason, King Mūrdhagata caused a rain of gold coins to fall within his own palace for seven days."
At that time, King Śatānīka again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
For what reason was that King Māndhātṛ able to exercise the sovereignty of a Wheel-Turning King over the four great continents and even reach the Heaven of the Thirty-three?"

The Buddha said, “Great King! In the distant past, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world, named Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.”
This Buddha, teaching and transforming sentient beings through the True Dharma, proceeded in succession until he reached the city of Pūrṇamati.

At one time, the Tathāgata entered the city to beg for alms. There was a merchant leader named Viśvakarman who, seeing the Tathāgata walking about begging for food, marveled at his sublime and rare marks.
With a pure heart, he took some green mung beans, placed them into the bowl, and offered them to the World-Honored One.

At that time, four beans entered the bowl; one rotated, struck the bowl, and made a rattling sound before falling to the ground, while the remaining beans likewise spilled out and scattered upon the earth.
At that time, having seen these signs, the merchant leader gave rise to a pure mind and made a vow in verse, saying:
"By this cause of vast generosity, May I attain the Buddha’s spontaneous wisdom of the world;
May I swiftly cross the stream of birth and death, And deliver all those not yet delivered by previous Buddhas."
The Buddha said: "Great King!

At that time, although the merchant leader offered only a small amount to the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Vipaśyin, because his mind was pure, four beans entered the Buddha’s bowl at that moment; later, as a result of this retribution, he attained the rank of a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) ruling over the four great continents."
If one of those beans strikes the bowl, makes a sound, and only then falls to the ground, its subsequent karmic retribution will enable it to reach the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Furthermore, Great King!
If that one bean does not fall to the ground but remains within the bowl, its subsequent retribution will surely make it the sovereign of the heavens.
Because he fell to the earth, he ruled only over the human realm and did not become the Lord of Devas.
Great King!
That caravan leader was none other than King Mūrdhaja.

Because the roots of goodness planted by the Buddha were embraced by that World-Honored One’s great compassion, he attained a great fruit of retribution, possessed a great reputation, and had great majestic radiance.
Therefore, Great King!
Any wise person should, according to their capacity and as is appropriate, practice various acts of giving toward the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
As it has been taught, one should train accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of King Mūrdhaja, Scroll Six.
